newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Norway sees growth continuing, inflation low.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Norway sees growth continuing, inflation low.

text.p: The Norwegian statistics office said on Thursday it expected the country's economy to continue to show strong growth this year and saw no signs of it overheating in 1998.

In a new forecast, Statistics Norway (SSB) kept unchanged from a first-quarter report its official projection for overall GDP in 1997 at 3.1 percent. The government department upgraded estimates for 1998 GDP to 4.2 percent from three percent in the February report.

"The rise in the business cycle in the Norwegian economy is now in its fourth year....," SSB's report said. "A strong increase in oil investment contributes to driving the growth while impulses from the traditional exports appear to be weaker this year than last year."

But the bureau's national account figures for first-quarter overall GDP -- a rise of 0.5 percent year-on-year and a fall of 0.1 percent from the fourth quarter 1996 -- took the market by surprise, according to analysts.
"The first quarter was surprisingly low but some of this may be attributed to a run-down in inventories," said Jon Eriksen at London-based I.D.E.A.

"The new forecast should be reassuring to the market because the statistics office does not see any signs of the economy overheating. Private consumption seems surprisingly well-behaved despite lower interest rates and rising income," he said.

SSB downgraded estimates for private consumption in 1997 to 2.5 percent against 3.1 percent in the February report. It attributed the revision to a levelling out of car sales despite lower interest rates over the past two quarters.

The bureau brought into line with the Finance Ministry and the Central Bank its estimate for consumer price (CPI) growth in 1997 to 2.4 percent. In its February outlook it indicated 1997's CPI at 1.8 percent mainly due to a strong appreciation in the Norwegian crown at the beginning of the year.
Both Norges Bank and the Finance Ministry have forecast inflation this year at around 2.5 percent.

The SSB said employment was expected to reach record high levels and forecast unemployment at 4.2 percent this year and at 4.0 percent in 1998. It warned that with such low jobless rates there was a danger of strong wage growth in the future although this had not been apparent following this year's wage settlements.
